introduction: Comfort, comfort my people, says the Lord through Isaiah. Today's readings announce good news: God is coming to save his people, and a voice cries out to prepare his way. In the Gospel, John the Baptist appears in the desert, calling people to repentance. As we light the second Advent candle, let us listen to that voice, and ask God to straighten the paths of our lives so that Christ may come to us.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: God is patient with us and wishes all to come to repentance. Let us pray to him with humble and hopeful hearts.
intentions: For the Church: that, like John the Baptist, she may prepare the way of the Lord by her preaching, her witness and her call to conversion. Let us pray to the Lord.
For peoples living through war, exile or disaster: that they may hear God's word of comfort and receive help from those who can give it. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have been away from the sacraments for a long time: that this Advent may draw them back to God's mercy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who are anxious about the future: that they may trust in the Lord, for whom a thousand years are like a day. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our community: that our words and deeds may comfort the sorrowful and prepare a way for Christ in our homes and workplaces. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Father of mercy, you speak tenderly to your people and call us to turn back to you. Hear our prayers, and make straight the paths of our hearts for the coming of your Son. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: A voice in the wilderness
reflection.body:
The second part of the book of Isaiah opens with words spoken to exiles far from home: "Comfort, comfort my people," says your God. Their exile is ending. A voice calls out to build a road through the desert, to fill in the valleys and lower the mountains, because God himself is coming to lead his people home like a shepherd carrying the lambs in his arms.

Mark begins his Gospel with that same prophecy. He does not start with shepherds or a manger, but with a man in the desert, dressed in camel's hair, calling Israel to repentance. John the Baptist is the voice, and he points away from himself: one more powerful is coming, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit.

Repentance can sound like a harsh word, but here it is part of the good news. To repent is to clear a road so that God can reach us. Every valley filled in is a hope restored; every mountain levelled is a pride laid down; every crooked path made straight is a habit of sin abandoned. God does the coming; we prepare the way.

The second reading speaks to people who wondered why the Lord seemed slow to return. Peter answers that "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." God is not slow, he says, but "patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance." The time we are given is a gift of mercy.

This Advent, where does the road need clearing in our own lives? Perhaps a relationship that needs forgiveness, a confession we have postponed, a habit that crowds out prayer. The Church offers the Sacrament of Reconciliation especially in these weeks. Let us not waste the time God gives. Let us prepare the way, so that the One who comes to comfort his people may find a straight path to our hearts.
